E1412.summary: In the later Appendix, Atwood's name for the shape-shifting life sought in the work, which she says is very hard to discover.
E1412.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says “The Protean life is very difficult of discovery” [APP ¶171]. Its last shape, she indicates, is a tree [APP ¶171].

E1413.summary: Atwood's figure for the one ever-changing universal entity of life, the subject of the work, identified with Mercury, the quintessence and the mercury of the Philosophers.
E1413.body:
Atwood uses Proteus as an image of the one subject in all its changing forms. In Part I she says “For Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36], citing the verse “Etherial, watery, earthy general soul, Immortal Fire! Even all the world is thine And pars of thee, O Proteus, power divine;” [I.2 ¶35]. She equates it with the Mercury and the quintessence: “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37]. In a footnote Proteus is the image of the one agent that is a serpent on earth, a fish in water and a bird in air, “yet is, not withstanding, One throughout the multiformity of nature” [I.3 n55].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) makes the same identification. Proteus is “the one universal entity of life, the omnia in omnibus before manifestation and individuality, the thing of which you may assert everything; Proteus.” [APP ¶138]. All descriptions of the Matter refer to it, and the work is said to be mechanical as well as alchemical, using instruments and vessels. It is also the world's “dissolved essence which is the mercury of the Philosophers, Proteus.” [APP ¶144].

Identities asserted: = Mercury, = quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; = one universal entity of life, = omnia in omnibus [APP ¶138]; = mercury of the Philosophers [APP ¶144].

E1414.summary: The field in which an adept cited by Atwood claims to have manual experience.
E1414.body: Atwood cites an adept's claim to “his own manual experience in the proto-chemistry of Hermes” [II.1 ¶11]. The packet gives no further explanation. Compare protochemistry and Protochemic Artifice.

E1415.summary: The practical art through which, according to Vaughan, the true foundation is found; Atwood sums up its whole performance as solution, sublimation and fixation.
E1415.body: In a passage attributed to Vaughan, a knowledge of this art comes before the philosophy of Wisdom: “a knowledge of the Protochemic Artifice; for that by means of this, and this only, the true foundation is discoverable” [II.1 ¶26]. Atwood, in her own voice, reduces it to three operations: “All that is performed in the Proto-chemic artifice may be comprehended in three terms” [III.2 ¶64]. These three terms are solution, sublimation and fixation.

E1416.summary: The protochemistry of Hermes, which Atwood says is the ground of Vaughan's discourse on the nature of man.
E1416.body: Atwood says that Vaughan's discourse on the nature of man is “grounded on the protochemistry of Hermes” [I.1 ¶74]. The term is not explained there. Compare proto-chemistry of Hermes and Protochemic Artifice.

E1417.summary: A biblical book Atwood quotes in support of seeking Wisdom and Self-Knowledge, and which she applies to the Mercury or water of the work.
E1417.body: Atwood cites Proverbs ii, 4, 5 in support of the call to Self-Knowledge: “If thou seekest for her as silver, and searchest for wisdom as for hidden treasures” [I.3 n46]. She uses Proverbs 8, introduced “as Solomon says”, for the worth and promises of Wisdom: “I love them that love me, and those that seek me early shall find me” [IV.3 ¶47; IV.3 n21; IV.3 n24]. She applies Proverbs iv, 8, 9 to the Mercury or water, which crowns the one who exalts her: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n8]. In each case Atwood quotes the text approvingly.

E1418.summary: Quoted by Atwood in support of the view that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.
E1418.body: Atwood quotes the Psalmist with approval: “I called upon the Lord, exclaims the Psalmist, and He heard me out of His holy temple” [III.4 ¶28]. She uses the line to show that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.

E1419.summary: Praised in the Appendix for their depth of Divine experience, which Atwood says the Mystics have neglected.
E1419.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Psalms are praised for their “surpassing depth of Divine experience”, and Atwood says the Mystics have neglected them [APP ¶97].

E1420.summary: Commentator on the Chaldaic Oracles whom Atwood cites on material rites, on the Mysteries as Initia, and on apparitions and introspection in the Chaldaic rites.
E1420.body: Atwood cites Psellus' commentary on the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the view that the soul is perfected by material rites together with divine illumination: “there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites” [II.1 ¶51]. She cites him again as having said that the Mysteries were called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In Part II, ch. 3 she uses his commentary (footnoted as “Pesllus de Oraculis”) on the apparitions of the Chaldaic rites, superinspection among them, as empty products of the soul's passions: “mere appearances, having no substance, and therefore not signifying anything true” [II.3 ¶20; II.3 n15]. She also contrasts “the Introspection which Psellus speaks of”, the formless Divine Light, with Superinspection in Hades [II.3 ¶46]. In all these places she uses him as support.

E1421.summary: Atwood's name for false seekers who followed receipts literally, without theory, in search of gold, as opposed to the true adepts.
E1421.body: Atwood sets the pseudo-alchemists against the true adepts. Their motives were “as those of the pseudo-alchemists, on the other hand, were reckless and despicable” [I.1 ¶41]. They took the receipts literally and, with no theory, worked with mineral sulfur, mercury and salt to make gold: “The pseudo-Alchemists dreamed of gold, and impossible transformations” [II.1 ¶6].

E1422.summary: The threefold separated essence that equals the whole dissolved compound it comes from; it is known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.
E1422.body: Atwood describes the Psychical Quintessence as “being in its own threefold segregated essentiality equal to the whole dissolute compound whence it arises” [III.2 ¶44]. It casts off what is superfluous, and she reads Pythagoras' hecatomb for his theorem as a symbol of its discovery [III.2 ¶44]. Identity asserted: = Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine (“that miraculous Psychical Quintessence, known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.2 ¶44]).

E1423.summary: Mentioned only once in the Appendix, where his astronomy is compared with Newton's.
E1423.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Ptolemy appears only in a comparison between his astronomy and Newton's [APP ¶122].

E1424.summary: In the Appendix, the higher Cause of life, which Reason reaches through secondary causes; Atwood also says the earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross.
E1424.body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes that “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110], and does not explain this further. Elsewhere she identifies the term with “the higher Cause, the punctum saliens of life” [APP ¶152]. Reason reaches it by way of secondary causes and there consciously finds its own roots. Identity asserted: = higher Cause [APP ¶152].

E1425.summary: In Crollius' account, the separated and purified medicine that is to be given to our bodies.
E1425.body: Speaking in Crollius' voice, the passage describes separating and purifying the medicine “that the pure crystalline matter may be administered to our bodies” [III.1 ¶10].

E1426.summary: The universal matter that subsists about Intelligibles and mediates between causes and their gross effects; the Theurgic Art makes it manifest, and in the Appendix it is the first, passive product of the work.
E1426.body:
In Part III Atwood describes “a certain pure matter subsisting about Intelligibles which is universal” [III.2 ¶46]. It is the origin of all vital and corporeal existence. It is hidden but can be made manifest to sense, and the Theurgic Art makes it manifest. It is connascent with the gods and receives Divinity. She also calls it “a certain pure and divine Matter mediately subsisting between primary and secondary causes and their gross effect” [III.2 ¶49].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds that, according to Lully, pure matter is not found on earth, and that “You may find out in Plotinus how that pure matter is generated.” [APP ¶43]. There it is the first product of the work: “a pure matter which is passive, having no power of perfecting itself; it is the attractive power” [APP ¶182]. Identity asserted: = the attractive power [APP ¶182].

E1427.summary: The purification of the soul, of which Atwood says Will is the greatest part; for the Paracelsians, the separation of the pure life from impurity, as metal from ore.
E1427.body: Atwood says that “Will is the greatest part of purgation” [II.2 ¶13], where purgation means the purification of the soul. In a passage given in the voice of the Paracelsians, purgation separates the pure life from the impure: “by a due purgation, the pure life is separated, as metal from the dark and sordid ore” [III.1 ¶10].

E1428.summary: The cleansing of souls, which Servius says the Bacchic rites served and which was a chief benefit of the Mysteries.
E1428.body: Atwood quotes Servius on the function of the Bacchic rites: “the sacred rites of Bacchus pertained to the purification of souls” [II.2 ¶5]. In the same paragraph the benefits of the Mysteries are given as “moral enlightenment and purification of life” [II.2 ¶5].

E1429.summary: The stage of the Mysteries that follows the revealing of the Medial Life; it restores the rule of reason and frees the inclination from sense before the deeper initiations.
E1429.body: Atwood places the Purificative Rites after the revealing of the Medial Life. They were rites “which were designed also to restore the monarchy of reason in the soul” [II.2 ¶20], and they prepare for the final initiations. The deeper mysteries require them, because after them comes “the inclination being already freed from the dominion and all the superficial progeny of sense” [II.3 ¶9].

E1430.summary: The agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward; Atwood identifies it with Isis.
E1430.body: Atwood describes the purified spirit or intelligence as the agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward. Identity asserted: = Isis (“the purified spirit or intelligence, that is Isis” [III.1 ¶23]).

E1431.summary: The decay and death that, according to Atwood, comes before every new form: linked with blackness (the ‘gate of blackness’, the ‘blackness of the night’), in which the matter dies and corrupts before it rises again.
E1431.body:
Atwood states that “putrefaction precedes the generation of every new form into existence” [I.3 n42], and links it with the ‘gate of blackness’. In the crow image she explains: “The blackness of the night is the putrefaction of the same” [I.3 n12]. The matching ‘clearness of the day’ is resurrection to a relative purity. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the darkened matter “lives in the putrefaction” [I.3 ¶48], and its dark clouds are changed.

In Part III Atwood applies the term to the decay of the vital vapour under the ferment. More generally, she applies it to the death and corruption that every life passes through before rising better, as a seed does: “Does not the grain putrefy in the moist earth before it springs?” [III.1 ¶30]. Morien, quoted in Part IV, describes the earth as having its water drawn off and returned again and again “until the earth is completely putrefied” [IV.1 ¶41]. The earth is then corrupt, without its Form, and dead for a season.

Identity asserted: = blackness of the night [I.3 n12].

E1432.summary: Atwood's name for the vital experiment, through which powers, the regenerative original and temptations were revealed to conscience.
E1432.body: Atwood uses the phrase for the vital experiment: “by this pyrotechnical induction, powers were revealed to conscience” [IV.4 ¶9]. What was revealed included the regenerative original and the temptations.

E1433.summary: A term Crollius pairs with physic, saying the two cannot be separated, in the context of trial by fire.
E1433.body: In a passage given in Crollius' voice, and in the context of trial by fire: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated” [III.1 ¶10].

E1434.summary: Greek philosopher whom Atwood cites on Wisdom, on initiatory ordeals and on the Tetractys; she reads his hecatomb symbolically as the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence.
E1434.body:
Atwood names Thales and Pythagoras among the early Greek philosophers who sought eastern wisdom, and notes that their writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She cites Pythagoras' definition of Wisdom as “the science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39; II.1 n36]. She also uses him as an example of the long preparations and ordeals required before admission to the deeper mysteries, and of the purifying of disciples' souls [II.2 ¶11].

She reports that Aristotle criticized him for explaining essence by number [III.2 ¶40]. She then reads his hecatomb, offered for the right-angle theorem, as a symbol of the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence [III.2 ¶43; III.2 ¶44]. She identifies the Conjunction with “that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer, spelled “Pythagorus”), his Tetractys is obtained by theurgic multiplication and is the kind of ens that underlies the stone. Atwood calls it “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108]. Throughout, Atwood uses him as support.

E1435.summary: Cited in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries bring about assimilation and final contact with the first principle.
E1435.body: Atwood cites the Pythagoreans in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries lead to assimilation and final contact with the first principle [II.2 ¶5].

E1436.summary: A precept Atwood quotes as a warning to would-be practitioners, alongside ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.
E1436.body: Atwood quotes the Pythagoric precept “Neither break a superficies” [IV.3 ¶56] as a warning to would-be practitioners and sets it beside the counsel ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.

E1437.summary: Impossible by natural means, Atwood says, but demonstrated supernaturally by transmuting the hypostatic relations; whoever finds it perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature.
E1437.body: Atwood writes that “the Quadrature of the Circle was supernaturally demonstrated; which naturally it cannot be” [III.3 ¶30]. It is demonstrated only by transmuting the hypostatic relations. The one who finds it has resolved all things into one Principle and perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature [III.3 ¶30].

E1438.summary: In the Appendix, to give something specific quality and form: essence is qualitated by Ideas, and the speech of Mind qualitates in the pure Ether.
E1438.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: “essence is qualitated, i.e., specificated, and receives form from Ideas” [APP ¶37]. Elsewhere she writes: “The speech of Mind uttered into the pure Ether qualitates and specificates.” [APP ¶64]. Identity asserted: = specificate [APP ¶37].

E1439.summary: The elements as they exist at their source; they multiply into distributive powers whose remote subjects are the sensible elements.
E1439.body: Atwood describes the source as “making elements there to subsist as qualitative virtues, which, multiplying into being, become distributive powers” [III.2 ¶38]. The remote subjects of these powers are the sensible elements.

E1440.summary: In the Adept's words, the fourfold through which the Ternary is reduced; it is identified with the four elements.
E1440.body: In a passage given in the voice of an Adept, the instruction is to “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18]. Identity asserted: = four elements (“the Quaternarius, or four elements, as some call them” [IV.2 ¶18]).

E1441.summary: Van Helmont's white sand, which Atwood describes as showing itself in a vital soil that no spade or mattock has ever pierced.
E1441.body: Atwood describes Van Helmont's Quellum, his white sand, as “manifesting itself forth in a vivid vital soil, which spade or mattock never pierced” [III.2 ¶8].
